summary: Describes how to use the RSAES-OAEP key transport algorithm with the Cryptographic Message Syntax. In enveloped data, the content is encrypted and the content-encryption key is separately protected for each recipient, and this document says how RSAES-OAEP does that protecting. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: A secret message is locked with a key, and that key must reach the reader. This memo says how to lock the key itself with a particular public-key method so only the right person can open it.

subtitle: How to lock the one-time content key of a CMS message with RSA using OAEP padding, which closes the Million Message Attack hole.

tldr.problem: PKCS #1 Version 1.5 RSA key transport is vulnerable to adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks (the Million Message Attack), especially in interactive request-response uses.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines how CMS enveloped-data wraps the content-encryption key for each recipient with RSAES-OAEP from PKCS #1 Version 2.1, including the algorithm identifier, its parameters, certificate conventions and S/MIME capability encodings.
tldr.outcome: CMS gains a key transport method that resolves the attack at the algorithm level instead of relying on protocol countermeasures. It is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 3560 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 3447 for the algorithm itself.

sections.title: Why Replace PKCS #1 Version 1.5
sections.content:
PKCS #1 Version 1.5 specifies a widely deployed form of RSA key transport. It is vulnerable to adaptive chosen ciphertext attacks, often called the Million Message Attack. An attacker needs an oracle that answers hundreds of thousands of adaptively built ciphertexts, telling the attacker whether each decryption succeeded or failed.

The RFC says the attack is significantly less feasible in store-and-forward settings such as S/MIME, and RFC 3218 described countermeasures for CMS. It is more feasible when key transport is an intermediate layer in an interactive request-response system. SSL and TLS implementations could include countermeasures, but at the protocol level.

The RFC argues that, for long-term assurance, it is prudent to adopt an improved technique rather than embed countermeasures in protocols. PKCS #1 Version 2.1 (RFC 3447) supersedes RFC 2313 and recommends Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding (OAEP) for RSA key transport. This document applies it to the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). PKCS #1 versions 1.5 and 2.1 need the same RSA public key information, so one certified key can be used with either technique.
sections.eli5: The old way of locking the key could be tricked if a bad guy could try a huge number of fake locks and watch which ones the receiver complained about. The new way is built so that trick does not work.

sections.title: Enveloped-data Conventions
sections.content:
A CMS enveloped-data object holds the encrypted content plus a wrapped content-encryption key for each recipient. RSAES-OAEP wraps the key for one recipient. Software MUST follow the enveloped-data rules in the CMS specification, and a content-encryption key MUST be randomly generated for each enveloped-data instance.

For the EnvelopedData fields, the version MUST be 0, 2, or 3. The originatorInfo field is not used by RSAES-OAEP but MAY be present for recipients using other key management algorithms. recipientInfos MUST be KeyTransRecipientInfo, and contentEncryptionAlgorithm MUST be a symmetric encryption algorithm identifier. unprotectedAttrs MAY be present.

In KeyTransRecipientInfo, the version MUST be 0 when the recipient is identified by issuerAndSerialNumber and 2 when it is identified by subjectKeyIdentifier. The recipient's certificate MUST contain an RSA public key, which MUST be at least 1024 bits long. The encryptedKey is the content-encryption key encrypted under that public key. For a Triple-DES content-encryption key, implementations MUST adjust the parity bits to odd parity for each octet of each DES key before encrypting.
sections.eli5: The message is locked with a fresh one-time key, and a copy of that key is locked separately for each reader using their own public lock. Each reader opens only their own copy.

sections.title: Algorithm Identifier and Parameters
sections.content:
RSAES-OAEP is the RSA encryption scheme of RFC 3447, where the message being encrypted is the content-encryption key. Its algorithm identifier is the object identifier id-RSAES-OAEP, and the parameters field MUST be present and hold RSAES-OAEP-params.

That structure has three optional fields, each with a default:

  • hashFunc: the one-way hash function. Default is SHA-1. Implementations MUST support SHA-1 and MAY support others.
  • maskGenFunc: the mask generation function. Implementations MUST support MGF1, which takes its own hash function in its parameter. Default is MGF1 with SHA-1.
  • pSourceFunc: the source of the encoding parameters P. P is represented with id-pSpecified, and the default is an empty string. Implementations MUST support a zero length P.

A common rule governs all three. An implementation that encrypts MUST omit the field when the default value is used. An implementation that decrypts MUST recognize both the explicit default identifier and an absent field as meaning the default.
sections.eli5: The lock has three settings, and each has a normal setting. If you use the normal setting you leave it out, and the reader knows to assume it.

sections.title: Certificate Conventions
sections.content:
A certificate user needs to know what form of key transport the owner of an RSA private key associates with the public key. The RFC therefore augments the X.509 profile of RFC 3280 with two ways to label the key.

If the owner does not want to limit the key to RSAES-OAEP, the rsaEncryption object identifier is used in the subject public key information, and its parameters MUST contain NULL (see RFC 3279). If the owner wants to restrict the key exclusively to RSAES-OAEP, the id-RSAES-OAEP identifier MUST be used, with RSAES-OAEP-params as the parameters.

Either way, the key itself is encoded the same way, as a DER-encoded RSAPublicKey (a modulus and a public exponent) inside the subjectPublicKey bit string. If a keyUsage extension is present on a certificate carrying id-RSAES-OAEP, it MUST contain a combination of keyEncipherment and dataEncipherment, though both SHOULD NOT be present. A user of such a certificate MUST use the key only for RSAES-OAEP and MUST use the parameters in the certificate.
sections.eli5: A certificate can say 'this key opens any kind of RSA lock' or 'this key opens only the new safe kind of lock, with these exact settings'. If it says the second, everyone must follow it.

sections.title: Announcing Support in S/MIME
sections.content:
S/MIME defines an SMIMECapabilities signed attribute (RFC 2633) that lists algorithms the sender can support. Software building a signed object MAY include it to announce RSAES-OAEP support.

With all defaults, the capability entry MUST carry the id-RSAES-OAEP identifier and an empty SEQUENCE as parameters, and it MUST be DER-encoded as the hexadecimal string 30 0D 06 09 2A 86 48 86 F7 0D 01 01 07 30 00. With non-default settings, the entry MUST carry the full RSAES-OAEP-params sequence.

The RFC also fixes the DER encodings for three common non-default cases: SHA-256 for both the hash and MGF1, SHA-384 for both, and SHA-512 for both. Each is defined in the ASN.1 module in Appendix A.
sections.eli5: A person can attach a note saying which kinds of locks they can open. The memo spells out exactly how to write that note, byte by byte, so every program reads it the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations must protect both the RSA private key and the content-encryption key. Losing the private key may expose every message protected with it, and losing a content-encryption key exposes that message's content. Key generation needs good random numbers, because a weak pseudo-random number generator leaves an attacker a small set of possibilities to search; RFC 1750 gives guidance.

An RSA key pair should be used in only one scheme, so a weakness in one cannot damage the other. A key pair used for RSAES-OAEP should not be used for other purposes, and should always be used with the same RSAES-OAEP parameters.

SHA-1 is required for interoperability, but the RFC notes that the best known collision attacks on it are generic attacks of complexity 2^80, so it gives a security level of no more than 80 bits in signature schemes. A 1024-bit RSA key and SHA-1 both give about 80 bits, which a NIST guideline suggested was adequate for most applications until 2015. For more, longer keys and SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 are likely candidates. The RFC recommends choosing a hash whose length in bits is at least twice the desired security level, and suggests using the same hash for hashFunc and maskGenFunc to reduce implementation errors, though it is not required.
sections.eli5: Guard your private key and your one-time key like house keys. Do not use one key for lots of different jobs. If you need a stronger lock later, pick bigger keys and stronger hash recipes.
